newsitem.title: FINLAND: Amer conversion clarifies group - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Amer conversion clarifies group - analysts.

text.p: Finnish sporting goods group Amer Oy's proposal to convert vote-strong K-shares to A-shares will clarify the group for investors, boost liquidity and may help the group to streamline itself, analysts said on Tuesday.

Amer has struggled with poor profitability in its key sporting goods units and has capital tied up in its tobacco unit -- where its roots lie -- and the Time/System unit which has kept it from focussing fully on the core business, they said.

Amer announced it planned to abolish its unlisted K shares, which have given four Finnish associations over 90 percent of voting control, converting every K-share to 1.2 A-shares. The four main owners' voting stake would fall to 13 percent.
"After this, it will surely become easier to make (divestment) decisions," said Postipankki analyst Teemu Lahkela.

Amer has said that of this year's net sales, 62 percent will come from the Wilson golf and tennis equipment unit, 20 percent from its skiing equipment unit Atomic, 11 percent from licensed tobacco manufacture and seven percent from the Time/System unit, which makes time planning calendars.

Analysts agreed the new ownership structure was likely to boost international interest in the share, and Lahkela said that even after an initial rise of over seven percent to 100 markka, the stock could add some 20 percent more.

"I think if there will be signs of strong demand around the autumn's (sporting goods) product launches, it is quite possible that the share could rise to 120-130 markka, even quite soon," Lahkela said.
Aktia Bank analyst Ritva Ojala said the arrangement would boost liquidity in the share.
"This is positive from the point of view of A-shareholders. Liquidity will improve," Ojala said.
The average daily trade volume this year up to April has been 51,051 shares or 5.16 million markka.

The K-shareholders have had an agreement to offer their shares to the other K-shareholders, but they will gain from the conversion since they will now be able to sell them bit by bit on the stock market, analysts said.
"In a sense this is technical, but -- as the company says -- it will make it more attractive because there won't be any owner with a dominant position," Ojala said.

The K-shareholders -- The Finnnish Association of Graduate Engineers TEK, The Student Union of the Helsinki School of Economics and Business Administration, The Finnish Association of Graduates in Economics and Business Administration (SEFE) and the Land and Water Technology Foundation -- tried to sell their K-shares last year but talks failed.
"This is evidently plan B," said Interbank analyst Sari Gronbarj.
